idea: A wireless smart sprinkler controller that replaces a home's irrigation timer and adjusts watering to local weather, controlled from a phone app

found.text: EPA estimates more than 28 million US homes have in-ground sprinkler systems that typically schedule watering with a clock-based controller.
EPA says replacing a clock-based controller with a WaterSense labeled weather-based controller can save an average home nearly 7,600 gallons of water a year.
A product reviewer describes Rachio and Orbit B-hyve as being in a two-way race for smart sprinkler market share.
Established smart controllers list at or below $200: Rachio 3 8-zone normally $199 at Home Depot, Rain Bird ST8 $160, Orbit B-hyve 6-zone $90-$115.
Some water utilities offer rebates for smart controllers; one buyer reported paying $15 for a Rachio after a water rebate.
SkyDrop tried to move features advertised as free behind a monthly subscription.
A University of Minnesota Extension study found 75 percent of homes with irrigation systems had at least one broken sprinkler.
At $200 one-time, the product would be priced at the top of an established category, so it needs a reason to win beyond weather-based scheduling, which incumbents already offer.
Broken heads and leaks could be a stronger pain point to build around than scheduling, since a smart schedule does not fix a broken sprinkler.

unknowns: What share of the 28 million homes already own a smart controller.
How often homeowners replace their irrigation controller (replacement cycle).
How many homeowners program their own controller versus relying on a landscaper or irrigation contractor.
Current US unit sales of smart controllers and each brand's share.
How many water utilities offer rebates today and how large they are.
Rachio's direct price on rachio.com (the product page shows no price to scripts).
How current the competitor prices are: the Rachio deal post is from April 2026, the GearBrain roundup from April 2025, and the Rain Bird price from a 2020 review.

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: Homeowners will pay $200 for a new brand when Rachio and B-hyve already do weather-based watering at the same price or less.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: The sourced prices show incumbents at $90-$199, and rebates can bring them near zero.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Ask 5 homeowners who bought a smart controller what they paid, what else they considered, and why they chose it.

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: Homeowners with clock-based timers feel enough pain to replace a working timer.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: EPA says most such homes still use clock-based controllers, which may mean the problem is not urgent to them.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Ask 5 homeowners with old timers when they last changed the schedule and what, if anything, went wrong.

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: The homeowner, not a landscaper or irrigation contractor, chooses and installs the controller.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: If contractors decide, a consumer app and retail channel would miss the buyer.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Ask homeowners who set up or replaced their current controller, and talk to 2 irrigation contractors about what they install.

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: A one-time price with no subscription can fund ongoing weather data and app costs.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: SkyDrop tried to add a subscription after launch; cloud costs continue after the sale.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Model per-user cloud and weather API cost for 10 years and compare it to gross margin at $200.

interview_script.intro: Thanks for talking with me. I'm learning how homeowners look after their lawn watering. There are no right answers, and I'm not selling anything.

questions.question: Tell me about the last time you changed your sprinkler schedule. What made you do it?
questions.listening_for: How often they touch the timer, and whether weather or water bills trigger changes.

questions.question: Who set up your current sprinkler controller, and when?
questions.listening_for: Whether the homeowner, a builder, or a contractor chooses and installs controllers.

questions.question: Tell me about the last time something went wrong with your sprinklers.
questions.listening_for: Broken heads, leaks, overwatering in rain, dead patches, and what it cost them.

questions.question: What did you spend on watering your lawn last summer, including water bills and repairs?
questions.listening_for: Whether water cost is a felt pain and how large it is.

questions.question: Have you ever looked into a smart or Wi-Fi sprinkler controller? What happened?
questions.listening_for: Brands they know, why they bought or did not buy, price objections, rebate awareness.

questions.question: If you own a smart controller, how did you choose it, and what do you wish it did?
questions.listening_for: Unmet needs incumbents leave open, and what made them pick a brand.

questions.question: How do you handle watering restrictions or rebates from your water utility today?
questions.listening_for: Whether utilities shape what they buy and when.
